hero.basedOn: A BMJ analysis article pooled two meta-analyses: 281 studies from 36 countries where people filled in the Yale Food Addiction Scale questionnaire. 14% of adults (12% of children) scored at the 'food addiction' level.
hero.caveat: A questionnaire score, not a diagnosis, and samples were mostly not national. The adult meta-analysis's own abstract reports 20% across its 272 studies, including clinical groups.
hero.numberCheck: 14% matches the BMJ text. Its source for adults, Praxedes 2022, gives 20% in its abstract (55% in people with binge eating). The 14% adult split was not visible in that abstract.

ref.cite: Gearhardt AN, Bueno NB, DiFeliceantonio AG, Roberto CA, Jimenez-Murcia S, Fernandez-Aranda F (2023). Social, clinical, and policy implications of ultra-processed food addiction. BMJ 383:e075354.
ref.quote: A recent analysis of two systematic reviews including 281 studies from 36 different countries found the overall pooled prevalence of food addiction using YFAS was 14% in adults

stats.line: For US adults aged 19 to 39, about 54% of daily calories come from ultra-processed food.
stats.mirror: Men whose meals come from a wrapper, a box or a drive-through.

basis.who: US youth and adults; this figure is adults aged 19-39
basis.n: national sample (exact n not given on the page)
basis.measured: Share of calories from ultra-processed food (NOVA groups), from one day's 24-hour diet recall interview. Men 53.3%, women 52.7% (all adults).

stats.caveat: This is what most people eat; it is not a sign of addiction. One day's recall can miss or misreport foods.

ref.cite: Williams AM, Couch CA, Emmerich SD, Ogburn DF (2025). Ultra-processed food consumption in youth and adults: United States, August 2021-August 2023. NCHS Data Brief No. 536.
ref.quote: Adults ages 19–39 consumed 54.4% of calories from ultra-processed foods.

stats.line: About 2 in 100 US men have had binge-eating disorder at some point. Fewer than half ever sought treatment for it.
stats.mirror: Men who eat until it hurts, then hide the wrappers.

basis.measured: Lifetime binge-eating disorder by a structured psychiatric interview (WHO CIDI, DSM-IV rules). 43.6% of people with it sought treatment specifically for it.

stats.caveat: Old data and older diagnostic rules. Lifetime means 'ever', so it includes men who have since recovered.

ref.cite: Hudson JI, Hiripi E, Pope HG, Kessler RC (2007). The prevalence and correlates of eating disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. Biological Psychiatry 61(3):348-358.
ref.quote: Lifetime prevalence estimates of DSM-IV anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating disorder are .9%, 1.5%, and 3.5% among women, and .3% .5%, and 2.0% among men.

stats.line: Counting milder cases too, about 4 in 100 US men have had a binge-eating pattern at some point.
stats.mirror: Men who binge often but think 'it's not a real problem'.

basis.measured: Lifetime 'any binge eating' (full disorder plus below-threshold cases) among men: 4.0%; below-threshold alone: 1.9%.

stats.caveat: Self-reported in an interview, years later. Below-threshold binge eating is not a diagnosis, and the cut-off is the interview's own.

ref.cite: Hudson JI, Hiripi E, Pope HG, Kessler RC (2007). The prevalence and correlates of eating disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. Biological Psychiatry 61(3):348-358.
ref.quote: Table 1, Male column: 'Subthreshold binge-eating' 1.9 (se 0.5); 'Any binge-eating behavior' 4.0 (se 0.7)

stats.line: Across 14 countries, only 38% of people who'd had binge-eating disorder ever got treatment for an eating disorder.
stats.mirror: Men who have never told anyone about the binges.

basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.when: published 2013 (survey years not stated in fetched text)
basis.measured: Share of people with lifetime binge-eating disorder who ever received treatment specifically for eating disorders. 57.7% got treatment for some emotional problem.

stats.caveat: Mostly richer countries. Treatment is self-reported and recalled.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Smaller proportions of lifetime cases (BN 47.4%, BED 38.3%) ever received treatment specifically for eating disorders.

stats.line: Binge-eating disorder usually starts in the late teens or early 20s; the middle age of onset was about 19.
stats.mirror: Men whose bingeing began at uni or the first job.

basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.when: published 2013 (survey years not stated in fetched text)
basis.measured: Age when symptoms first started, recalled in a structured interview. Median 19.3 years for binge-eating disorder (18.0 for bulimia).

stats.caveat: Age is remembered, often years later. The US survey (Hudson 2007) found a median of 21.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Median age of onset is in the late teens to early 20s for both disorders (full text: medians: 18.0 vs. 19.3)

stats.line: Cravings and food cues explain about 11% of later eating and weight gain; food pictures and videos pull as hard as real food.
stats.mirror: Men who get hungry watching food videos at midnight.

basis.who: children and adults, lean and heavy
basis.measured: Link between reacting to food cues or craving, and later eating or weight gain (r = 0.33, medium). Same size across body weight, age and dieting.

stats.caveat: A link, not proof that cues cause weight gain. 11% means most of what you eat is explained by other things.

ref.cite: Boswell RG, Kober H (2016). Food cue reactivity and craving predict eating and weight gain: a meta-analytic review. Obesity Reviews 17(2):159-177.
ref.quote: we found an overall medium effect of food cue reactivity and craving on outcomes (r = 0.33, p < 0.001; approximately 11% of variance)

stats.line: On ultra-processed food, people ate about 500 more calories a day and gained about 0.9 kg in two weeks.
stats.mirror: Men who 'eat normally' but keep gaining.

basis.who: weight-stable adults, mean age 31, average BMI 27; 10 men, 10 women
basis.measured: Food eaten when free to eat as much as wanted, weighed by staff. Meals matched for calories offered, sugar, fat, fibre and salt.

stats.caveat: Only 20 people, in hospital, for two weeks. They also ate faster on ultra-processed food (17 kcal a minute more).

ref.cite: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metabolism 30(1):67-77.
ref.quote: Energy intake was greater during the ultra-processed diet (508 ± 106 kcal/day; p = 0.0001)

stats.line: People who eat more ultra-processed food have about 1.5 times the odds of anxiety and about 1.4 times the odds of sleep problems.
stats.mirror: Men who feel wired, tired and on edge.

basis.who: adults and children in observational studies
basis.measured: Odds of current anxiety (odds ratio 1.48) and sleep problems (1.41) with higher versus lower ultra-processed food intake.

stats.caveat: Observational: anxious or sleepless people may eat more junk, not the other way round. Evidence quality rated low. Odds, not risk.

ref.cite: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, et al. (2024). Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ 384:e077310.
ref.quote: higher risks of prevalent anxiety outcomes (odds ratio 1.48, 1.37 to 1.59; low)

stats.line: Once it starts, binge-eating disorder lasts about 4 years on average, the middle value across 14 countries.
stats.mirror: Men who have been 'starting Monday' for years.

basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.when: published 2013 (survey years not stated in fetched text)
basis.measured: Years with the disorder, from recalled onset to recovery or interview. Middle country 4.3 years; middle half of countries 1.0 to 11.7.

stats.caveat: A wide range, from about 1 to 12 years. Recalled, and mixes treated and untreated people.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Persistence is slightly higher for BN (6.5 years; 2.2-15.4) than BED (4.3 years; 1.0-11.7).

stats.line: After therapy for binge eating, mostly CBT, about half of people who finish stop bingeing completely, and it held at follow-up.
stats.mirror: Men who think nothing will ever stop the binges.

basis.who: adults with binge-eating disorder; 65 treatment groups, 40 of them CBT
basis.measured: Share with zero binges at end of treatment: 50.9% of finishers, 45.1% of all who started; follow-up 50.3% and 42.3%.

stats.caveat: A 2026 update of 52 trials found 43%, with no gains in 40 years. Zero binges is a strict bar; many others improve partly.

ref.cite: Linardon J (2018). Rates of abstinence following psychological or behavioral treatments for binge-eating disorder: meta-analysis. International Journal of Eating Disorders 51(8):785-797.
ref.quote: treatment-completers who achieved abstinence at posttreatment was 50.9% (95% CI = 43.9, 57.8); this estimate was almost identical at follow-up (50.3%

stats.line: In guided CBT self-help, people who cut binges by 70% or more by week 4 were more likely to stay binge-free long term.
stats.mirror: Men starting a programme and wondering if it's working.

basis.where: USA (US research teams; sites not named in abstract)
basis.measured: Binge-free rates after interpersonal therapy, CBT guided self-help or weight-loss treatment, by whether binges dropped 70% by week 4.

stats.caveat: Slow starters are not doomed: in interpersonal therapy, fast and slow responders did equally well.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Hildebrandt T, Agras WS, Wilfley DE, Wilson GT (2015). Rapid response in psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 83(3):649-654.
ref.quote: the predictive value of rapid response, defined as ≥70% reduction in binge eating by Week 4, was determined for remission from binge eating

stats.line: Slips are common: between one and four years after group CBT, about 1 in 4 people slid back into binge eating.
stats.mirror: Men who binged again and think they failed.

basis.who: adults with binge eating disorder and overweight, about 80% women, mean age about 45
basis.measured: Relapse to binge eating between the 1-year and 4-year check-ups, after 20 weekly group sessions of CBT or interpersonal therapy (IPT: 10%).

stats.caveat: One trial, mostly middle-aged women. Even so, most were binge-free at 4 years.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Bishop ME, Stein RI, et al. (2012). Long-term efficacy of psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. British Journal of Psychiatry 200(3):232-237.
ref.quote: 6 (24.0%) patients in the CBT and 3 (10.0%) in the IPT group relapsed

stats.line: People who cut down on junk food remember days 2 to 5 as the hardest.
stats.mirror: Men who quit sugar and feel awful by day three.

basis.who: adults aged 19-68 who had cut down on highly processed food in the past year; 51.9% women
basis.measured: Recalled 'withdrawal' symptoms (mood, cravings, body) during a past attempt to cut down, on a new scale.

stats.caveat: Memory of a past attempt, online volunteers. A later trial (107 people) found cutting junk caused no more withdrawal than a normal diet.

ref.cite: Schulte EM, Smeal JK, Lewis J, Gearhardt AN (2018). Development of the Highly Processed Food Withdrawal Scale. Appetite 131:148-154.
ref.quote: symptoms assessed by the ProWS were reported as most intense between days 2-5 during an attempt to cut down

stats.line: In a trial of 107 people, cutting ultra-processed food caused no more withdrawal than a normal calorie-cut diet.
stats.mirror: Men afraid cutting junk will feel like detox.

basis.design: secondary analysis of a randomised trial
basis.who: adults with obesity on a weight-loss diet
basis.n: 107 adults (51 normal diet, 56 diet plus cutting ultra-processed food)
basis.measured: Withdrawal scale scores on days 1, 3, 5 and 15. Difference 4.34 points, not statistically significant.

stats.caveat: Small, all dieting, only 16% had 'food addiction'. A small extra effect can't be ruled out. Anxious people reported more withdrawal in both groups.

ref.cite: Lopes NGDS, Ferreira CS, Silva-Junior AE, et al. (2026). Impact of dietary ultra-processed food restriction on withdrawal symptoms in individuals with obesity undergoing a weight loss diet. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN 76:105105.
ref.quote: A total of 107 participants were randomized (51 to ER-G and 56 to ER-UPF).

stats.line: On unprocessed food, the same people ate less without trying and lost about 0.9 kg in two weeks.
stats.mirror: Men who think losing weight means fighting hunger all day.

basis.who: weight-stable adults, mean age 31, average BMI 27; 10 men, 10 women
basis.measured: Body weight on each diet, free to eat as much as wanted. On unprocessed food the fullness hormone PYY rose and hunger hormone ghrelin fell.

stats.caveat: In hospital with meals cooked for them; 20 people; two weeks. Real life with shops and stress is harder.

ref.cite: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metabolism 30(1):67-77.
ref.quote: participants gaining 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.009) during the ultra-processed diet and losing 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.007) during the unprocessed diet

stats.line: Four years after group therapy for binge eating, about 64% were fully free of binge eating.
stats.mirror: Men who want proof that it stays fixed.

basis.who: adults with binge eating disorder and overweight, about 80% women, mean age about 45
basis.measured: Interview-rated full recovery from binge eating 4 years after 20 weekly group sessions (CBT 52.0%, IPT 76.7%). 80.0% binged below the diagnostic level.

stats.caveat: One trial, mostly middle-aged women, and only those who came back. Weight stayed about the same.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Bishop ME, Stein RI, et al. (2012). Long-term efficacy of psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. British Journal of Psychiatry 200(3):232-237.
ref.quote: with full recovery from binge eating in 64.4% of patients

stats.line: Over five years, most young women with binge-eating disorder recovered: only 18% still had an eating disorder at the end.
stats.mirror: Anyone who thinks bingeing is a life sentence.

basis.who: women aged 16-35 at the start, found in the community
basis.where: not stated in fetched abstract (UK research group)
basis.measured: Any eating disorder of clinical severity, checked every 15 months for 5 years. Few sought treatment.

stats.caveat: Women only, small. Weight still rose: 39% were obese at 5 years.

ref.cite: Fairburn CG, Cooper Z, Doll HA, Norman P, O'Connor M (2000). The natural course of bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder in young women. Archives of General Psychiatry 57(7):659-665.
ref.quote: the proportion with any form of clinical eating disorder declining to 18% (7 of 40) by the 5-year follow-up

rejected.claim: Regular meals (no skipping) reduce binge eating, with a number
rejected.why: No fetched study gave a number for regular eating on its own; it is one part of CBT. Not used.
Abstract gives no effect size; girls only. Already in the page's whatWorks; no new number.

rejected.claim: Fat plus carbohydrate foods are valued more than either alone (DiFeliceantonio 2018)
rejected.why: Abstract has no sample size or number. Not used.

rejected.claim: Hilbert 2019 meta-analysis (81 trials, 7,515 people): CBT remission rate
rejected.why: Abstract gives effect sizes, not a remission percentage; used Linardon 2018 abstinence rates instead.

rejected.claim: Ultra-processed food raises depression odds 1.55x (Menon 2026, NHANES 2021-23)
rejected.why: Measured ultra-processed food only by added sugar; weak method. Not used.

rejected.claim: Lane 2024 umbrella review: deaths from heart disease and all causes
rejected.why: Death counts left out on the owner's rule; only anxiety and sleep used.

rejected.claim: Praxedes 2022: food addiction 20% overall, 55% in people with binge eating
rejected.why: Checks out but already in the page's numbers; used in the hero numberCheck instead.

rejected.claim: Hero line '14% of adults meet the threshold for food addiction'
rejected.why: Matches the BMJ text, but the cited adult meta-analysis abstract says 20%. Say 'about 1 in 7 to 1 in 5, depending on the study set', or cite both.
